slides: Open by presenting de Rham cohomology as the bookkeeping system for global obstruction. Locally, closed forms often look exact; globally, loops, covers, compact support, and top-degree integration can detect the obstruction. The lecture moves from closed modulo exact to homotopy invariance, Mayer-Vietoris, and degree.

Use the proof dependency map as the chapter's reading guide. The complex starts with d squared equals zero, which lets exact forms sit inside closed forms. Pullback gives functoriality, the homotopy operator proves homotopy invariance, Mayer-Vietoris computes from covers, and top-degree cohomology supports degree theory.

This is the first obstruction example. The angular form on the punctured plane is closed because d omega is zero, but its loop integral is 2*pi. If it were globally exact, Stokes would force the integral around a boundaryless loop to vanish, so the nonzero period detects the hole.

Homotopy invariance depends on an explicit cochain homotopy, not just geometric intuition. In the cylinder picture, the interval direction turns endpoint change into an exact term. The notebook's symbolic test uses g(s)=s^3-2s and gets h(dg)=-1, matching g(1)-g(0).

This slide translates cohomology into linear algebra. A cochain is closed when the next coboundary kills it, exact when it comes from the previous image, and cohomology is the quotient. The finite models show b1 equals one for the circle but zero for the interval and the filled triangle.

Mayer-Vietoris is the computation engine. Cover S^1 by two arcs with a two-component overlap: the local H1 groups vanish, but the mismatch of constants on the overlap has a one-dimensional cokernel. The rank check records rank alpha one, rank beta one, and H1 of the circle equal to one.

Top degree is where hypotheses matter most. Compactness, orientability, and compact support change the answer. The table keeps the theorem cases visible: compact connected orientable manifolds have top de Rham group R, while noncompact orientable ordinary top cohomology and nonorientable top cases vanish under the listed hypotheses.

Degree theory is the payoff from top cohomology. For circle maps z to z^k, integrating the pullback of the angular class and counting signed preimages give the same integer. The examples k=2, k=1, k=-1, and a constant map all agree across the two definitions.

Use the applied lab to reinforce invariance under composition and homotopy. Changing k changes both the integral degree and the signed-preimage count together. Composing z squared after z inverse produces degree minus two, showing that degree multiplies and records orientation reversal.

Close by connecting the proof tools. The de Rham complex turns calculus into a quotient, periods detect nonexactness, homotopy operators kill homotopic differences, Mayer-Vietoris computes from simple covers, and top-degree integration turns smooth maps into homotopy-invariant integers.
